title: The Bracket Clock: Form and Purpose
body:
Specifications: A bracket clock is a spring-driven table clock made to sit on a wall bracket, with a carrying handle on top and a case typically 25 to 40 centimetres tall. The name comes from the bracket it stands on, not from the shape of the case. Most examples date from the late seventeenth century onward and use a short pendulum behind the dial.

Mechanism: The going train is driven by a spring barrel, regulated by a short pendulum and an anchor or verge escapement. Because the pendulum is short, the beat is fast, often more than 100 beats per minute, and the movement is compact enough to fit a case that can be carried by its handle.

Maintenance: Keep a bracket clock level on its bracket, wind it at the same time each week, and dust the case with a soft dry cloth. Never move the clock while the pendulum is swinging, and never force the hands backwards past the striking point.

Build and restoration: Restoration starts with photographing the movement in place, then removing the dial and hands before lifting the movement from the case. Tools: screwdrivers, hand puller, tweezers, pegwood, clock oil, and a beat amplifier or listening rod.

title: The Wall Bracket and Mounting
body:
Specifications: A wall bracket for a bracket clock is a wooden or metal shelf fixed to the wall with screws into solid masonry or a stud, sized to the clock's footprint plus a margin of at least 2 centimetres on each side. The bracket must hold the clock's full weight, typically 3 to 8 kilograms, without flexing.

Mechanism: The bracket does nothing to the timekeeping itself, but a bracket that flexes or tilts changes the clock's level, and a clock out of level will not keep an even beat. The pendulum must hang plumb, so the bracket top must be checked with a spirit level in both directions.

Maintenance: Check bracket fixings once a year and re-level the clock after any move. If the clock ticks unevenly, level the bracket before suspecting the movement.

Build and restoration: To fit a bracket, mark fixing points, drill, plug, and screw the bracket home, then level it and test it with a weight equal to the clock. Tools: spirit level, drill, wall plugs, screws, pencil, and tape measure.

title: Verge Escapement Bracket Clocks
body:
Specifications: Early bracket clocks, from about 1660 to 1700, used the verge escapement with a short pendulum or a balance, in a case about 30 centimetres tall with a brass dial. Verge bracket clocks are rare survivors and are valued as the earliest form of the type.

Mechanism: The verge is a vertical arbor with two pallets that alternately engage a crown wheel. Each swing of the pendulum or balance lets the crown wheel advance one tooth, and the recoil action makes the motion visibly jerky compared with the later anchor escapement.

Maintenance: Verge movements need regular oiling at the crown wheel pivots and pallets, and the crown wheel teeth must be checked for wear. Do not over-oil, since excess oil traps dust and forms grinding paste.

Build and restoration: Restoring a verge bracket clock means checking crown wheel tooth shape and pallet depth before any polishing, since over-polishing destroys the original geometry. Tools: pivot polisher, depthing tool, oilers, and magnification.

title: Anchor Escapement and the Short Pendulum
body:
Specifications: From about 1670 onward, bracket clocks adopted the anchor escapement with a short pendulum, usually 20 to 30 centimetres long, hanging behind the dial. The anchor's recoil is gentler than the verge's, and the short pendulum lets the case stay compact.

Mechanism: The anchor rocks with the pendulum and its two pallets alternately catch and release the escape wheel teeth. The pendulum's period follows T equals 2 pi times the square root of L over g, so a 25 centimetre pendulum beats at about 119 beats per minute.

Maintenance: Anchor bracket clocks should be oiled every three to five years at the escape wheel pivots and pallet faces. If the tick sounds uneven, the clock is out of beat and needs levelling or beat adjustment, not more oil.

Build and restoration: To set the beat, shift the crutch or the pendulum suspension until the ticks are evenly spaced, listening with the case closed. Tools: beat amplifier, screwdriver, pliers, and a timing app or beat counter.

title: Spring Drive and the Going Barrel
body:
Specifications: A bracket clock's going barrel holds a coiled mainspring, typically 15 to 20 millimetres wide, that stores about eight days of energy in an eight-day movement or one day in a thirty-hour movement. The barrel drives the centre wheel and the rest of the going train.

Mechanism: As the spring unwinds it turns the barrel, and the great wheel on the barrel arbor drives the centre wheel once per hour. A fusee was sometimes fitted to even out the spring's falling torque, but most bracket clocks use a plain going barrel with a stopwork that prevents over-winding.

Maintenance: Wind a spring-driven bracket clock gently until the stopwork resists, and never force the key past that point. A mainspring that slips or a clock that stops early in the week usually needs a clean and a new spring, not harder winding.

Build and restoration: Replacing a mainspring requires a spring winder and a barrel clamp, and the old spring must be let down in a controlled way before removal. Tools: spring winder, barrel clamp, gloves, eye protection, and mainspring gauge.

title: Hour-Striking Bracket Clocks
body:
Specifications: A striking bracket clock sounds the hour on a bell or gong, with one blow at one o'clock rising to twelve blows at twelve o'clock. The strike train is separate from the going train and is released by the motion work once per hour.

Mechanism: The strike train is governed by a countwheel or rack-and-snail mechanism. In a rack-and-snail clock the snail on the hour wheel sets how far the rack falls, and the rack's teeth count the blows; in a countwheel clock a slotted wheel spaces the strikes.

Maintenance: If the strike count disagrees with the hands, do not move the hour hand alone; let the clock strike through, or use the repeat cord if fitted, until the count matches. A clock that strikes wrongly usually has a bent rack tail or a dirty countwheel.

Build and restoration: Servicing the strike train means cleaning the countwheel slots or the rack teeth and checking the warning pin. Tools: screwdrivers, tweezers, pegwood, oil, and a strike-count chart.

title: Quarter-Chiming Bracket Clocks
body:
Specifications: A quarter-chiming bracket clock plays a short tune at each quarter hour, most famously the Westminster quarters, on four or five bells or gong rods. The chime train is a third train beside the going and strike trains, and the case is often larger to hold the bells.

Mechanism: A chime barrel with raised pins lifts hammers in sequence as it turns, sounding the quarters at 15, 30 and 45 minutes past the hour and the full sequence with the hour strike on the hour. The Westminster sequence uses the notes E, D, C and G in a fixed pattern.

Maintenance: Chime trains need clean barrels and hammers that fall freely; a hammer that sticks gives a dull note or no note. Oil the chime barrel pivots sparingly and keep the hammers clear of dust and case lining.

Build and restoration: Rebuilding a chime barrel requires noting every pin position before cleaning, since a misplaced pin changes the tune. Tools: pin chart, tweezers, hammer-setting tool, oil, and a tuning fork or pitch reference.

title: Pull-Repeat Bracket Clocks
body:
Specifications: A pull-repeat bracket clock repeats the last hour, and often the quarters, when a cord hanging from the case is pulled. Repeat work was fitted so the time could be heard in the dark, and it is a hallmark of better bracket clocks.

Mechanism: Pulling the cord winds a small repeat spring and releases the strike train under rack control, sounding the hour just struck and then the quarters if the mechanism includes them. The repeat is independent of the normal strike, so it can be used at any moment.

Maintenance: Keep the repeat cord free of knots and fraying, and pull it smoothly rather than jerking it. If the repeat sounds the wrong hour, the rack is usually out of step with the snail and needs a clockmaker's adjustment.

Build and restoration: Repairing repeat work means tracing the cord path, the repeat spring, and the rack release in order, testing each step by hand. Tools: cord, tweezers, screwdrivers, magnification, and a repeat-test chart.

title: Grande Sonnerie Bracket Clocks
body:
Specifications: A grande sonnerie bracket clock strikes the full quarters and the hour at every quarter hour, automatically, without being asked. It is the most elaborate striking form, needing three trains and a large case, and it commands the highest prices among bracket clocks.

Mechanism: At each quarter the chime barrel plays the quarter tune and then the hour strike follows, so the clock sounds at 15, 30 and 45 minutes and on the hour with the full hour count. A selector usually offers grande sonnerie, petite sonnerie, and silent modes.

Maintenance: Grande sonnerie clocks should be wound fully and regularly, since the strike train does the most work of any bracket clock. If the clock is left unwound, the chime and strike trains stop at different points and the sequence can fall out of step.

Build and restoration: Rebuilding a grande sonnerie train requires assembling the chime, strike and going trains in order and testing the mode selector at every quarter. Tools: train diagram, tweezers, oil, screwdrivers, and patience.

title: Strike-Silent and Night Silence Controls
body:
Specifications: Many bracket clocks carry a strike-silent lever or a night-silence device that stops the strike, or the chime, between set hours, typically 10 at night and 8 in the morning. The lever moves a detent into the strike train's path so the release cannot fire.

Mechanism: Night silence works by a cam on the hour wheel that only allows the strike release to fall during daytime hours. The going train runs on regardless, so the clock keeps time silently and resumes striking in the morning without any adjustment.

Maintenance: Use the strike-silent lever only when the clock is not in warning, that is, not in the minutes just before the hour, or the lever may jam the release. If the silence fails, the cam or the detent spring is usually bent or dry.

Build and restoration: Fitting a silence lever means aligning the detent with the warning wheel and testing it through a full 24 hour cycle by hand. Tools: screwdrivers, bending pliers, oil, and a 24-hour test chart.

title: The Silvered Dial and Spandrels
body:
Specifications: Classic English bracket clock dials are brass plates with a silvered chapter ring carrying Roman numerals, Arabic five-minute marks, and a centre that may be matted or engraved. The corners carry cast spandrels, often of cherub heads or scrollwork, screwed through the dial plate.

Mechanism: The hour hand is driven by the motion work at one twelfth the speed of the minute hand, and both hands sit on squared arbors over the chapter ring. Subsidiary dials, when fitted, are driven by the same motion work through additional wheels.

Maintenance: Clean a silvered dial only with a soft dry brush, never with water or polish, since the silvering is thin and easily removed. Tarnish that will not brush away is best left alone; aggressive cleaning destroys value.

Build and restoration: Re-silvering a dial is a specialist job using silvering solution on a cleaned brass plate, with the numerals re-blackened afterwards. Tools: soft brushes, dial wax, silvering solution, and a dial template.

title: Mahogany and Ebonised Cases
body:
Specifications: Bracket clock cases are most often mahogany, walnut, or ebonised wood with brass mounts, a glazed front door, and sound frets in the sides or top. A typical case is about 35 centimetres tall, 25 wide and 18 deep, with a brass carrying handle on the top.

Mechanism: The case protects the movement from dust and draughts and shapes the sound of the bell or gongs, since the frets let sound out while the wooden panels colour it. The handle is fixed through the top with bolts and washers so the clock can be lifted safely.

Maintenance: Polish wooden cases with beeswax, not silicone spray, and keep them out of direct sunlight and away from radiators, which dry and crack veneer. Tighten a loose handle before carrying the clock, and always carry it by the handle with the other hand under the base.

Build and restoration: Repairing a case means gluing veneer with hide glue, matching the grain, and re-finishing with shellac or wax rather than modern varnish. Tools: hide glue, clamps, veneer saw, shellac, wax, and fine abrasive paper.

title: Bracket Clocks with Calendar Work
body:
Specifications: Some bracket clocks carry a calendar aperture showing the date, and a few add the day of the week or the month. The date wheel advances once per day from the motion work and must be corrected by hand at the end of short months.

Mechanism: The calendar wheel has 31 teeth and is stepped by a finger on the hour wheel once every 24 hours. A date aperture in the dial shows one numeral at a time, and a setting square on the dial back lets the owner advance the wheel without moving the hands.

Maintenance: Correct the date in the morning, never between 9 at night and 3 in the morning when the calendar finger is engaged, or the finger may bend. If the date jumps twice, the finger spring is weak or the wheel is dirty.

Build and restoration: Servicing calendar work means cleaning the 31-tooth wheel and checking the finger depth at midnight. Tools: tweezers, oil, screwdriver, and a calendar test chart.

title: Bracket Clocks with Moonphase Dials
body:
Specifications: A moonphase bracket clock shows the moon's age on a painted disc that turns behind an aperture, completing one cycle in about 29 and a half days. The disc carries two moons and a star field, and the aperture shape shows the moon waxing and waning.

Mechanism: The moon disc is driven from the motion work through a reduction gear of about 59 teeth, so it advances one tooth per day and one full moon per 29.5 days. The 59-tooth wheel gives the well-known approximation of two lunar months per wheel revolution.

Maintenance: Set the moonphase from a known new moon date, advancing the disc by hand to match, and correct it by one day every two or three years if the clock has the simple 59-tooth drive. Keep the painted disc dry and out of sunlight to protect the paint.

Build and restoration: Repainting a moon disc requires matching the original blue ground and silver stars, and the disc must be re-fitted so the moons centre in the aperture. Tools: fine brushes, moonphase paint, tweezers, and a lunar calendar.

title: Servicing a Spring-Driven Bracket Movement
body:
Specifications: A full service of a bracket clock movement means stripping the going, strike and chime trains, cleaning every wheel and pinion, re-bushing worn pivot holes, re-oiling, and testing the clock for at least a week. A service is due every five to eight years in normal home use.

Mechanism: Each train runs from its barrel through a series of wheels and pinions to its escapement or governor, and wear shows first at the barrel and centre pivots, which carry the most load. A clock that stops, runs fast, or strikes weakly usually has dirt, wear, or dried oil rather than a broken part.

Maintenance: Between services, wind regularly, keep the clock level, and listen for changes in the tick or strike. Do not oil a dirty movement from the outside; fresh oil on dirt only spreads the abrasive paste.

Build and restoration: A service bench needs a movement holder, cleaning machine or jars, bushing tools, and an oil set. Tools: screwdrivers, tweezers, pegwood, bushing machine, pivot polisher, and clock oil in several grades.

title: Beat Setting and Regulation of a Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: Beat setting makes the tick and the tock evenly spaced, and regulation sets the rate, by raising or lowering the pendulum rating nut. A bracket clock is in beat when the two sounds are equal, and in regulation when it gains or loses less than a minute a week.

Mechanism: The anchor escapement gives an equal beat when the crutch sits centrally so the pallets release symmetrically. Turning the rating nut down lengthens the pendulum and slows the clock, following the square-root law of the pendulum period.

Maintenance: Set the beat first by levelling, then adjust the rating nut by small turns, one turn at a time, and time the clock over a full week before adjusting again. Record each adjustment and its effect so the next service starts from a known point.

Build and restoration: Regulating tools are simple but precise: a beat amplifier, a timing reference, and a rating-nut key. Tools: beat amplifier, screwdriver, timing chart, and a reliable reference clock.
